title: Solar Power
objective: After this level you can explain how solar panels turn sunlight into electricity.
summary: Sunlight knocks electrons loose in a semiconductor cell, with nothing spinning. Panels make DC, so inverters turn it into AC. In 2025 solar passed wind worldwide.

cards.headline: In 2025, solar passed wind as a source of the world's electricity.
cards.body: It was the first time, according to the International Energy Agency. And solar does it with no turbine at all. As Level 8 pointed out, nothing spins: sunlight goes in, electricity comes out. So how does a flat panel pull that off?

cards.headline: Light knocks electrons loose
cards.body: A solar cell, or photovoltaic (PV) cell, is made of a semiconductor, like Level 5's LED. When it absorbs enough sunlight, electrons are knocked loose and move toward the cell's front surface. That builds up a charge imbalance, like the two ends of a battery. Connect the cell into a circuit and current flows. An LED turns electricity into light; a solar cell runs the trick the other way.

cards.fact: Solar cells make direct current, so an inverter turns it into AC.
cards.context: Remember Level 9: the grid runs on AC, while solar cells make DC. An inverter converts one into the other. Cells are wired into weather-tight panels, and panels are grouped into arrays. Edison's DC lost the War of the Currents, but every solar cell brings it back.

cards.headline: Better every decade
cards.body: The first practical solar cell came from Bell Telephone researchers in 1954. Efficiency, the share of sunlight a panel turns into electricity, has climbed steadily: commercial panels averaged under 10% in the mid-1980s, about 15% by 2015, and the best modules now approach 25%. One thing no panel can fix is sunset, so PV systems can charge batteries to supply power when the sun isn't shining.

cards.headline: Solar: switched on
learned: Sunlight knocks electrons loose in a semiconductor
Solar cells make DC; inverters turn it into AC
Bell researchers made the first practical cell in 1954

questions.prompt: What happens when a solar cell absorbs enough sunlight?

options.label: Electrons are knocked loose from its atoms
Water inside it boils into steam
options.rationale: Solar cells have no water and no steam.

options.label: A tiny turbine inside it spins
options.rationale: Nothing spins in a solar cell.

options.label: It stores the light as chemicals
options.rationale: That would be a battery's job.

questions.explanation: Sunlight knocks electrons loose; the charge imbalance drives a current when the cell is in a circuit.

questions.prompt: Why does a rooftop solar system need an inverter?

options.label: To point the panels at the Sun
options.rationale: An inverter converts current; it doesn't move panels.

options.label: To store power for the night
options.rationale: Batteries store power; inverters convert it.

options.label: To turn the panels' DC into the grid's AC
To cool the panels on hot days
options.rationale: Inverters change the kind of current.

questions.explanation: Solar cells make direct current; the grid and homes run on alternating current, so an inverter converts it.

questions.prompt: How is a solar cell related to Level 5's LED?

options.label: Both glow because a filament gets hot
Both need a spinning magnet inside
Both are semiconductors, working in opposite directions

questions.explanation: An LED turns electricity into light in a semiconductor; a solar cell turns light into electricity.
